11.0.0.en: Lazarus was a person beloved of the Lord, to Him be glory, along with his two sisters. His house served as a station where Christ would rest during His travels. The name "Lazarus" means: "God has helped." And the village of "Bethany" means: "house of affliction," and it is about 3 km from Jerusalem.

11.0.1.en: And the reference to the illness of Lazarus here is an introduction to the rest of the events of the chapter.

11.0.2.en: And the story of Mary's anointing Christ with perfume comes in detail in (ch. 12:3-8).

11.1.0.en: Christ was beyond the Jordan when the two sisters sent to Him, with the familiarity of love and family friendship, hoping for the healing of their brother. Christ did not need anyone to remind Him that He loved Lazarus. But what the two sisters said, and these words, are a kind of intercessory appeal, that Christ might come more quickly. And we learn from Mary and Martha, from what they did in sending a messenger to Christ, to send our prayers to Him on behalf of our sick loved ones, not only those whom we know in particular, but for all the sick in general.

11.2.0.en: "Not unto death": Christ's answer here is evidence of His divinity, for He answers the bearer of the urgent message, within the hearing of His disciples, that "this sickness is not unto death," and evidence also of His foreknowledge of all the events of this story that were to come. Indeed the Lord repeats what He had said before in (ch. 9:3) before the healing of the man born blind; which is that both illnesses were by a divine arrangement through which the Son's power to create eyes and to raise from the dead would be revealed.

11.3.0.en: "Jesus loved": it is an example of Christ's love for all His creation, especially these hearts and eyes that are attached to Him.

11.3.1.en: And St. John mentioned this love here, and affirms it, lest the reader hasten to say: how could the Lord Christ neglect the important message of the messenger about the illness of His beloved Lazarus, and stay for two days away, delaying?! For Christ loves, and this is a fact. And we must learn good spiritual things, which are God's wisdom in ordering the times; for our prayers are raised before Him the moment they are uttered. But the response and its timing depend on God's wisdom in ordering the times: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Eccl 3:1), and the delay sometimes brings more benefits... and may be a test of man's faith and trust in God... We also learn not to condemn people if they are late in asking after us, perhaps they had important matters that kept them from us, but rather to seek excuses for them.

11.4.0.en: And the loving heart of Christ responded, at the time He saw fit. So after the two days, He set out for Bethany in Judea, leaving Bethabara beyond the Jordan, taking with Him His disciples who would become witnesses of this great event.

11.5.s.en: (2) The disciples' fear of visiting Judea

11.5.0.en: The events of the Feast of Dedication, and the Lord's discourse about the flock and the Shepherd, and the Jews' attempt to stone the Lord Jesus or seize Him, were still present before the eyes of the disciples. Therefore came their objecting inquiry about going to Judea, and their fear for Christ, and for themselves, of the violence of the Jews.

11.6.0.en: What Christ said to the disciples in these two verses is by way of an illustrative parable; for Christ is the light of the day, and the hours of the day are the time of His appointed ministry on earth. Therefore, there is no need for fear, as long as it is day and I am with you. And Christ made this clear when He said: "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light" (ch. 12:35), as though He were saying do not fear, for no one will be able to harm you, because first I am with you, and second no one has authority over me because my hour has not yet come, so make your condition like that of one who travels by day and fears nothing, before the darkness comes.

11.7.0.en: "Our friend Lazarus": Christ expresses here the relationship of love that binds Him to Lazarus, and He included the disciples in it also.

11.7.1.en: But the spiritual meaning is that Lazarus alone was not what was meant, for Christ loves you, and loves me also, and loves all His children. Did He not call all of us in the Song of Songs by the name "my love"? You may call God in your prayer "my beloved." But do you also hear Him calling you beloved, and how great is its echo in your soul? Indeed He also calls you beloved before His disciples and all His saints.

11.7.2.en: "Sleepeth": Christ used this expression to teach us that the death that comes upon His children in the body is not death, but a quiet sleep followed by resurrection and eternal life.

11.7.3.en: Therefore, the Church in the prayer for the departed says: "It is not death for Your servants, but a departure." But death, for Christ, means perdition resulting from unbelief in Him, or rejection of His commandments, or the pride of man, or rejection of the sacraments of the Church, for this is the true death that is not followed by life, but by judgment.

11.7.4.en: "That I may awake him": a reference to His divine work in raising Lazarus from the dead. And the disciples did not understand this reference, but they would grasp its meaning after the miracle of the resurrection.

11.8.0.en: The disciples understood Christ's words literally, without reaching His meaning. And since their heartfelt desire still did not want to go to Judea, they offered his sleep as evidence of the beginning of his recovery... which indeed happens in many illnesses, such as fever, for the beginning of a long sleep precedes recovery... And in the face of this distance from understanding, Christ declared plainly His former meaning, which was the declaration of Lazarus' death in the body.

11.9.0.en: "I am glad for your sakes": the Lord was not glad at the death of Lazarus, but because of His knowledge of what would happen, for the raising of Lazarus would be a great cause of strengthening the disciples' faith in the face of the events of the cross, which had drawn very near. Also, there are many, besides the disciples, who would believe in Christ after this miracle... And He also makes clear the reason for His gladness... that He was not there at the time of his illness, because the miracle would have been of lesser account, and the disciples had seen repeated examples of it... but the effect would become greater when one who had been dead four days is raised.

11.10.0.en: The speech here is an aside, in a low voice, from Thomas, who is known for his doubt and anxiety, to the disciples.

11.10.1.en: As though Thomas were saying that the Teacher did not listen to our advice and our entreaty to Him. Consequently, the inevitable result is that the Jews will seize Him and us, and we shall all die together.

11.10.2.en: And what Thomas did then, many also do, those whose reason precedes their faith. And instead of believing the news of faith, they cause the simple to doubt their faith, for example by their mockery of miracles, or of the power of God, or of the authority of the saints.

11.10.3.en: O my God, do not make our minds obstacles and barriers that block the current of faith, but open our hearts, that we may receive and also proclaim Your great works.

11.11.s.en: (3) Christ is the resurrection and the life

11.11.0.en: "Four days": it is the period between Christ's informing His disciples of Lazarus' sleep, and His leaving beyond the Jordan for Judea. And Bethany is about 45 minutes' walk from Jerusalem. And as is the custom of most societies until now, many of the people of the village had gathered to console Mary and Martha in their house.

11.12.0.en: It is understood from the text that Christ did not go to the house of Lazarus, but a messenger told Martha, who went out quickly to meet Christ outside, and left Mary among the mourners, and Mary did not know, or else she would have gone out also with her. Her not knowing is clear from (v. 28), when Martha later told her "The Master is come."

11.13.0.en: With spontaneity and simplicity, Martha spoke what she felt, for she expressed her regret at Christ's absence at the time of her brother's illness, for she knew that His love for the person of Lazarus on the one hand, and His being considered a righteous prophet who had performed many miracles of healing before, and that whatever He asks of God is granted Him on the other hand, would have been enough to heal him and prevent his death. And her saying: "But I know, that even now," meant her expecting something from Christ, which was probably the raising of her brother, but she was not sure of that, as the rest of her speech shows.

11.13.1.en: And perhaps the most important thing we learn here from Martha is simplicity and frankness of speech, which are important elements that our prayers often lack. We must speak with God of everything we feel, whether distress or a request for help, or thanks for what He has bestowed on us; for sincerity and frankness are the basis of acceptable prayer.

11.14.0.en: A new contrast that St. John presents, as he is accustomed to bring out the great difference between what God intends and what man understands. For Christ makes clear here that Lazarus will truly rise, because the resurrection and the life are among the properties and authority of the only-begotten Son, which He grants to whom He wills of Himself. But Martha had not yet understood this divine dimension in the person of Christ. Therefore her answer, with what is firmly fixed in the minds of all people, was that her brother "shall rise again" also like everyone, "at the last day," that is, the day of the general resurrection of all people.

11.15.0.en: Christ answers here correcting the concepts, and declaring His divinity in His own power, that He is "the resurrection" and the source of "the life." And the resurrection is possible at any time according to His will and power, and not only on the last day as it is in people's minds, and everyone who dies in the body, like Lazarus, but "believes" in Him, "shall live," that is, will have eternal life. For bodily death does not touch the spirit at all, but the death of the spirit, by sin, is considered unbelief in Christ. Consequently, there will be for him no resurrection of life, but eternal judgment. And this faith makes us realize the secret of our fathers the martyrs' lack of fear of death. For death for the sake of the name of Christ, they considered the beginning of life, and a pledge of the true resurrection.

11.15.1.en: "I am the resurrection, and the life": an expression full of hope for every soul that still groans from the death of sin. For Christ declares to it that He is the secret of its resurrection and its life, if it wants resurrection from its death.

11.15.2.en: So come, let us present this Christ who raises up to every soul far from His Church, and we shall enjoy miracles of daily resurrection in His Church through the return of everyone who "was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found" (Lk 15:24, 32).

11.16.0.en: Faith in Christ adds another advantage for the one who believes in Him, which is not dying eternally, in completion of the meaning of the previous verse. For not only will the one who was dead live, but the one who is alive "shall never die." And this completion makes us realize the difference between the concept of death in the world on the one hand, and with God and His children on the other, as was previously made clear in (v. 25).

11.16.1.en: "Believest thou this?": the same question Christ asked the man born blind (ch. 9:35). And Christ affirmed, again and again, that faith in the person of the Savior is the basis of salvation, healing and gifts, the most important of which is the resurrection and not dying.

11.17.0.en: The declaration of Martha's faith comes here as a counterpart to Peter's declaration in (Mt 16:16) that Christ is the incarnate Son, who comes into the world for its salvation.

11.17.1.en: And St. John Chrysostom comments that Martha, like Peter, could not rise by herself to this level of declaration, but the Holy Spirit declared it through the tongue of Martha, as He declared it through the tongue of Peter. But the certain faith in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, as the Son of God the Savior, was completed after the Resurrection, and was revealed after the descent of the Holy Spirit on the disciples.

11.18.0.en: "Called Mary her sister secretly": that is, Martha returned to the house and informed her sister of Christ's arrival. And the word "secretly," perhaps she did not want to disturb the mourners. In another opinion, she feared that there might be enemies of Christ among the mourners to whom she did not wish to announce His coming. As for Mary, when she heard, her response was swift. And this is what we all need, that our response be swift to the calls of Christ to us, for we often err by postponing the response, and many opportunities of enjoying the meeting with the person of the beloved Christ are lost.

11.19.0.en: Christ did not enter the village or the house of Lazarus, for His aim was clear, which was the raising of Lazarus, and not consolation for his death. And Mary's going out with Martha from the house was noticeable to the Jews and the mourners, so they in turn rose up, following them, supposing they were going to the tomb, like the custom of many in weeping at tombs. And perhaps this was a divine arrangement, that the mourners should go out behind them, so that they might witness this unique miracle. And when Mary met Christ, she spoke like what Martha had said before (v. 21). But her worship at His feet is evidence of her great honor to the person of Christ, and also of her being crushed with grief at His not being there before her brother's death.

11.20.0.en: The sight of Mary's weeping and of the mourners gathered with her was an extremely moving sight, especially as it touched a person close to the heart of Christ. And since Christ was perfect God, able to raise Lazarus, He was also perfect man, bearing within Him all the tender feelings. And the expression "groaned in the spirit" means in Greek that He was not pleased or at ease. And the word "was troubled" also means in Greek a shuddering.

11.20.1.en: And it is a picture that clarifies the meaning of Christ's feeling for us, for He is tender of heart, He feels the pains of His children, He suffers and is distressed and shares their sorrows (Isa 63:9). And this in itself gives consolation to everyone who is in trial or distress.

11.20.2.en: And perhaps we also learn from this situation the positive Christian sharing with those who are in distress or deep sorrow, "weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15), and not to belittle or make light of people's feelings when they weep, but our weeping too is not wrong, as long as it does not exceed the limits of our faith and our hope of resurrection after death. For the wrong sorrow, against which God warns us, is the sorrow of those who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13).

11.20.3.en: "Jesus wept": it came as an expression of all that surged in His heart, and toward His feelings.

11.20.4.en: And perhaps we remember the words with which the Church prays in the Litany of the Sick: "Hope of those who have no hope, helper of those who have no helper, comfort of the fainthearted, harbor of those in the storm."

11.21.0.en: St. John continues to describe the scene for us, and relates the comments of the crowd. For some, when they saw the tears of the Lord Jesus, were moved by the degree of the Lord's love for the person of Lazarus. And others, whose words carried doubt about Christ's power, meaning that if what they had heard about His opening the eyes of a blind man was true, was He not able also to rescue and heal His friend, all the more?!

11.21.1.en: "Jesus therefore again groaning in himself": He felt uneasy, as a result of the surrounding atmosphere in general, and because of His approach to the place of the tomb, and also the talk of the Jews in (vv. 36, 37). And the tomb was a cave in the rock, as was the custom of people in burying their dead, either in natural or hewn caves, and they would close them afterward with a stone.

11.22.0.en: "Take ye away the stone": could not He who was able to raise the dead by a word also move the stone?! But this is God's way, who allows man to take part in the work. What is within man's power, God does not do. And the involving of man happened also in the filling of the waterpots with water at the wedding in Cana of Galilee (ch. 2:7), and also in the gathering of the baskets in the miracle of feeding the crowds (Mt 15:37; Mk 8:8).

11.22.1.en: And God's involving of man makes him a witness of God's work and plans. And it is an advantage enjoyed by whoever works in the field of the Lord's service, for he sees His works up close, and takes part in them. We also learn that, although salvation is a divine work in the first place, man also has a role in this salvation by his works, and by sharing with the saving grace of God through his striving.

11.22.2.en: "He hath been dead four days": that is, the impossibility of resurrection after decomposition and decay. And what is the use of taking away the stone except to stir up needless sorrows?

11.22.3.en: As for the spiritual meaning, the talk here is about the person who has died in sin, until his will has decomposed before it, and the works of the lusts of the flesh have become stinking; yet even this person, whom everyone supposes has no resurrection, has a resurrection through repentance, which turns the decay and stench of sin into precious perfume.

11.23.0.en: In (v. 4), the Lord indicates that the illness of Lazarus is not unto death, but for the glory of God. And here, the Lord Christ declares, with power, this glory, or at least one form of the glory of God, in absolute power, and the Son's victory over death, as an introduction to His own resurrection. And as for the expression "if thou wouldest believe," Christ links the beholding of glory to the condition of faith. For without faith, it is impossible to please Him. Therefore St. Matthew says: "And he did not many mighty works there (Nazareth) because of their unbelief" (Mt 13:58).

11.24.0.en: They took away the stone, with feelings of curiosity overcoming them over what was about to take place; the wavering of feelings here between doubt and certainty among the people is, we might say, natural, with the absence of the final declaration of Christ's divinity, and the presence of believing supporters and opponents in the surrounding crowd. After that Christ turns to speak with God the Father, and the purpose of this prayer, or audible speech, is "that they may believe that thou hast sent me." For Christ wants to use this unique event to declare what has been declared many times in the Gospel of John, that He is from the Father and in the Father, and the will is one between them, and to answer those who said earlier that He performed His miracles by Beelzebub (Mt 12:24; Mk 3:22; Lk 11:15). So here, He declares that the foundation is God and His will working in His Son.

11.24.1.en: And there is another purpose for us, which is that Christ teaches us the principle of constant prayer, especially before undertaking any work. And Christ also presents in His prayer the element of thanksgiving, with which the Church always teaches us to begin all our prayers.

11.24.2.en: "Thou hast heard me... thou hearest me always": this saying highlights the constant and continual agreement between the Son's request and the Father's response, for the Son's first work is the petition on behalf of His creation, through His shed blood, and the Father, who is one with the Son in will and essence, always accepts His petition. And Christ affirms this meaning in His discourse with His disciples: "Whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it" (ch. 14:13, 14).

11.25.0.en: "He cried with a loud voice": Christ's voice came out great and resounding, shaking the foundations of Hades, and commanding it to open its gates for the release of Lazarus' spirit from it, and defeating death that lay upon all mankind. And He commanded Lazarus to rise, and did not command him to rise in the name of the Father, to show that what the Father does, the Son also does with the same power and authority.

11.26.0.en: How great, one wonders, must have been the astonishment and bewilderment of those present before this dead man rising, after decay and decomposition lasting "four days"?! Yet Christ intervenes with His voice once more to rouse the crowd from its bewilderment, and commands some of them to loose him and let him go.

11.26.1.en: And as Christ had given man a role in taking away the stone, so here He also entrusts the soul raised from the death of sin to the care of the Church, priests and servants. For He has done His atoning work with it, and granted it forgiveness of sins and resurrection, but He left part of the work to the Church, which continues in its shepherding the completion of the work of the healing Physician. For when He raised the girl, He commanded that something be given her to eat (Lk 8:55). And Christ has deposited all His spiritual food in His Church, so whoever repents and does not partake continually of the food of life dies forever (ch. 6:53).

11.27.0.en: The situation remains as it is between those who accept the work of God and believe in it, and those who watch and deny. And this is what Christ said in the Gospel of our teacher Luke: "Neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead" (Lk 16:31). For the first group, the resurrection of Lazarus ran like a current through their bodies, and their faith in Christ grew great. But the others, their earthly attachment and their fear for their interests stood as a barrier that prevented their believing in this great event.

11.27.1.en: O my God, open my sight and my heart to see Your works, and do not let my mind or the desires of my heart be an obstacle that lessens my faith in all Your works.

11.28.0.en: The aim of the priests and Pharisees was clear, to be rid of the person of the Lord Jesus, who drew everyone to Him, and because of whom their fame and their power over the people had receded. Therefore, and because of the power of this miracle, they gathered a council with the intention already set to be rid of Christ (see ch. 5:18; 7:1, 25, 30, 44; 8:40, 59; 10:31-33, 39).

11.28.1.en: And they had nothing before them but to formulate the reasons that would support their decision, and justify it before themselves and before the people. So their minds hit upon a very flimsy political reason, which was that the crowds' following Christ would provoke the Romans and stir up disturbances, and the end would be the extermination of the Jewish nation. However, what condemns them most is their own admission that the Lord was performing many signs. And instead of this leading them to believe in Him, they sought to kill Him. And perhaps the sin of justifying judgments and actions is one we also fall into, as the priests and Pharisees did, and we care about what numbs our consciences and improves our image before people, forgetting God the true Judge, who searches the hearts and thoughts of all mankind... Blessed are those who cared to justify their conscience before God alone... "Blessed is he whom his conscience hath not condemned, and who is not fallen from his hope" (Sir 14:2).

11.29.0.en: Caiaphas was high priest, and was a relative by blood of Annas, the former high priest.

11.29.1.en: And the length of Caiaphas' tenure as high priest was 11 years, in which he was contemporary with all the events of the Lord Christ, and he was known in Jewish history as ignorant and hard of heart.

11.29.2.en: "Ye know nothing at all": thus Caiaphas began his speech, sheltering in his high office in the eyes of the rest, and as a suggestive introduction that what he would say was God's opinion, because the Law is sought from the mouth of the priest. So he came forward, as a man of religion and politics, offering what would set consciences at ease: "that it is expedient that one man (even if he is righteous) should die for the people." And what Caiaphas offered here was the formula that everyone was looking for in order to set their consciences at ease.

11.30.0.en: Caiaphas was not truly a prophet, but God put on his tongue what points to God's purpose and prior appointment, for God used him here to announce the course of events. As for what came in (v. 52), which is dying for the rest of the world to gather the children of God, this is outside Caiaphas' speech, and is a digression by St. John, by which he completes the declaration of God's purpose that Christ's death was not for the redemption of the Jewish nation only, but for the redemption of the whole world; and this is what came on the tongue of Christ Himself in (ch. 10:16) "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring."

11.31.0.en: This was the end of the session of the priests and Pharisees, for the decision had become clear, and what remained was to consult on how to carry it out and seize Christ.

11.32.0.en: The session ended, the news spread, and many learned of the decision of the secret council. And since Christ's hour had not yet come, and He is the only One who knows its time, the Lord preferred wisdom to declaring Himself, so He went away from the place of the inflamed events, and went to the city of Ephraim, a city now known as "al-Taybeh," about 20 km east of Jerusalem and the regions of the wilderness of the Jordan.

11.33.0.en: St. John begins here to bring us to the last section of his Gospel, for he prepares the reader for the first scene of the last Passover, with the Jews streaming from all parts of Judea to Jerusalem, days before the Passover itself, so that they might prepare for the Passover by offering purification sacrifices, because the Law forbade the defiled to touch the Passover lamb or eat it, so purification was necessary, especially for everyone who had become defiled.

11.33.1.en: My beloved brother... the Jews were careful to obey God by the necessity of purification before approaching the Passover lamb, which is a symbol of the true sacrifice of Christ... So what of people among us who approach the Body of our true God, and partake of it, without also being purified by true spiritual repentance, and by the practice of the sacrament of confession, in which they receive absolution, forgiveness and purification, not by water or by the sprinkling of an animal's blood, but by the Holy Spirit, God the Life-giver and Purifier?!

11.34.0.en: In these two verses there are two groups seeking the Lord Jesus, although their intentions and purposes differ; the first group: the simple people, who yearned to see this righteous One who had done all these signs, especially the sign of the raising of Lazarus from the dead. The second group: its motive was to lie in wait in order to seize Him, as a prelude to trying Him and killing Him. And this verse clarifies the verdict on which the council settled in (v. 53). The pouring of the perfume; Christ's entry into Jerusalem; Christ's discourse about His redemption and His judgment
